title: Produce word processing documents for business

lessons.title: Planning and creating business documents
lessons.html:
Word processing at work

Supervisors and administrators on farms, in seed operations and in abattoirs produce many documents: memos, letters to suppliers, reports to management, standard operating procedures, notices and meeting minutes. A word processor such as Microsoft Word, LibreOffice Writer or Google Docs makes it possible to produce professional, consistent documents quickly.

Plan before you type

  • Purpose: inform, request, instruct, record or persuade?
  • Audience: manager, worker, customer, government official?
  • Type of document: letter, memo, report, notice, form?
  • House style: does the company have a template, logo, font and layout rules?

Common business document types

DocumentUseKey layout features
Business letterExternal communication, such as to a seed supplierLetterhead, date, recipient address, reference, salutation, body, closing, signature
MemoShort internal messageTo, From, Date, Subject, brief body
ReportPresent findings and recommendationsTitle page, headings, numbered sections, tables, conclusion
NoticeInform many staffLarge clear heading, short text, date, contact person

Creating and saving documents

  1. Open the word processor and start a new document, or open the company template.
  2. Type the content first; format later.
  3. Save early with a meaningful file name, for example 2026-03 Seed intake report v1.
  4. Save in the correct shared folder so colleagues can find it.
  5. Save regularly and keep backups. Power interruptions can cause loss of unsaved work.

Use keyboard shortcuts to work faster: Ctrl+S save, Ctrl+C copy, Ctrl+V paste, Ctrl+Z undo, Ctrl+B bold, Ctrl+P print.

lessons.title: Formatting and layout
lessons.html:
Making documents look professional

Character formatting

  • Choose a clear font such as Arial or Calibri, usually 10 to 12 point for body text.
  • Use bold for headings or key terms, italics sparingly for emphasis, and avoid underlining large blocks of text.
  • Keep fonts consistent: no more than two font types in one document.

Paragraph formatting

  • Alignment: left-aligned is easiest to read; justified gives straight edges both sides; centred is for headings and titles.
  • Line spacing: single or 1.15 for letters; more space between paragraphs makes text easier to read.
  • Indents and tabs line up text neatly; do not use repeated spaces.
  • Bulleted and numbered lists break up information. Use numbers for steps in a procedure.

Styles and headings

Use built-in heading styles (Heading 1, Heading 2) rather than formatting each heading by hand. Styles keep the document consistent and allow an automatic table of contents in longer reports.

Page layout

  • Set paper size to A4 and suitable margins.
  • Use portrait for most documents; landscape for wide tables.
  • Add headers and footers with the company name, document title and page numbers.
  • Insert page breaks to start new sections on a new page.

Tables

Tables organise data such as a seed lot list: lot number, cultivar, mass, germination percentage and storage location. Insert a table with the right number of columns, add a bold header row, adjust column widths and apply borders or shading for clarity.

Inserting objects

You can insert the company logo, a photo of a defect, a chart from a spreadsheet, or a simple diagram. Resize objects proportionally and place them close to the text that refers to them.

lessons.title: Editing, checking and printing
lessons.html:
Getting it right before it goes out

Editing tools

  • Cut, copy and paste to move text.
  • Find and replace to change a word throughout, for example changing a supplier's name.
  • Undo and redo to reverse mistakes.
  • Track changes and comments so a manager can suggest edits that you then accept or reject.

Proofreading

Spell check helps, but it does not catch everything. 'From' typed as 'form' will not be flagged. Proofread carefully:

  1. Run the spelling and grammar check, and set the language to English (South Africa).
  2. Read the document slowly, ideally on a printout or aloud.
  3. Check names, dates, figures, product codes and amounts against the source.
  4. Check that headings, fonts and spacing are consistent.
  5. Ask a colleague to check important documents.

Print preview and printing

Always use print preview before printing. Check margins, page breaks, that tables do not split awkwardly and that the page count is what you expect. Choose the correct printer, number of copies and page range. Print double-sided for internal documents to save paper.

Saving in other formats

Save as PDF when sending documents externally so the layout cannot change and the document is harder to edit. Keep the original editable file for future updates.

Version control and confidentiality

Use version numbers or dates in file names. Store documents in the correct folder, protect confidential documents such as payroll or disciplinary letters with access controls, and do not leave confidential printouts on the printer.

Key points

  • Plan the purpose, audience and type of document before typing.
  • Use consistent fonts, heading styles and lists for a professional look.
  • Use tables, headers, footers and page numbers to organise information.
  • Proofread carefully; spell check does not catch every error.
  • Use print preview, save as PDF for external documents and keep versions organised.
